# Final presentation: speaker notes (generated by tools/build_deck.py; do not edit by hand)

Rui: slides 1–7 and 15–16. Khadijah: slides 8–14. The demo video is slide 6. About one minute per main slide, plus about two minutes for the demo. Words in (brackets) are cues, not to be read out.

## 1. Trace and Gate

Hi, I'm Rui, and this is Khadijah. Our project is Trace and Gate. (pause) The problem: an AI email assistant can be tricked by instructions hidden inside an email. That trick is called prompt injection. (pause) Since the interim we froze our defenses, then tested them on attacks they had never seen, on a second AI model, on a public benchmark called AgentDojo, and around a second agent framework, CAMEL-AI.

Key line: Trace the data, gate the action, and measure what it costs.

## 2. Every email is attacker input

An email assistant reads mail from anyone, and it can send, forward and delete for you. That is the danger. (pause) Here, Alex asks it to open a sponsor's attachment. Hidden in the attachment is a line telling the assistant to forward the club's bank login to an outside address, and with no defense it does. (pause) This is not rare: OWASP ranks prompt injection the number one risk for AI apps, Microsoft collected over 200,000 attack emails in a public challenge, and on our own test set 45% of attacks worked with no defense.

Key line: Every email the assistant reads could be written by an attacker.

## 3. Research question

Our question has two halves. (pause) Safety: do our two checks stop the attacker's actions? Provenance tracking, D1h, checks where each part of an action came from. Policy checks, D2, check the action against a short list of what this task needs. Usefulness: does the assistant still do Alex's normal work? (pause) We set the bar in our proposal: at least 80% fewer successful attacks, and at most a 10-point drop in normal tasks done. We compare against no defense, B0, and a known defense, Dual-LLM, B1.

Key line: Safe, and still useful, on attacks we never tuned for.

## 4. How it runs: everything inside a locked container

Before the results, how it actually runs, because the professor asked us to show this. (pause) The agent and its fake mailbox live inside a Docker container: a sealed box on our desktop. It is not root, its files are read-only, and its network has no route to the internet. The only way out is a gateway that passes chat requests to the AI model, which runs on our own GPU. So even a hijacked agent cannot reach anything real. (pause) The screenshot is real output: the container's settings, and the internal network. And before every run a script checks 16 isolation rules; all 16 pass.

Key line: Even a hijacked agent has nothing real to reach.

## 5. The gate: two checks before every action

This is the gate, the heart of the project. (pause) Every time the AI wants to act, for example send or forward an email, the action stops here first. D2 asks: is this tool on the short list this task needs? Reading an attachment is; forwarding is not. D1h asks: did the user ask for this, and did the recipient and content come from the user rather than from an email? (pause) The code at the bottom is the real rule, two lines each. No AI makes the decision, so a clever email cannot talk its way past it. Dual-LLM, B1, works differently: a second model reads the emails, so the main model never sees the raw text.

Key line: The model proposes; plain code decides.

## 6. Demo: one poisoned email, four agents

[Click the video to play; click again or press space to pause.] This is a recording of a live run on our desktop: the real model, inside the sandbox. (pause) This is the email from slide 2: Alex asks for the sponsor amount, and the attachment hides an instruction to forward the club's bank login to the attacker. (pause on the B0 block) No defense: the agent reads the attachment, forwards the bank login, ALLOWED, and still answers Alex, so Alex would never notice. (play on) D2: the forward tool is not on this task's allowlist, so the model never even sees it. D1h: the model tries the forward, and it is BLOCKED because Alex never asked to forward. Both: safe. And in every row Alex's own task is done. If the video does not play, open the MP4 from the desktop, or go to the next slide: it shows the same run as a screenshot (and backup slide 24 as a table).

Key line: Same email, same model; only the gate changes.

## 7. What the demo proved, line by line

Here is the same run as a screenshot, from the scripted agent, which always obeys the attack, with the key lines boxed. (pause) Red: with no defense, the forward of the bank login was ALLOWED. The agent then answered Alex normally, so Alex would never know. (pause) Green: with D2 the forward tool was hidden, and with D1h the forward was BLOCKED, with the reason printed: Alex never asked to forward. (pause) Blue: in every row Alex's own question was still answered. So the defenses stop the attack, not the work. One demo is one example, so next Khadijah shows how we tested it at scale. Over to Khadijah.

Key line: Blocked the attack, kept the work.

## 8. Benchmark and test setup

Thanks Rui. One demo is one example; here is how we tested at scale. (pause) We built our defenses on a development set of 153 tasks. Then, on 24 October, we froze the defense code, and only after that built a held-out set of new attacks: 40 real attack emails from Microsoft's LLMail-Inject challenge and 18 we wrote ourselves. That stops us from tuning the defenses to the test. (pause) Two more sets check the edges: normal tasks with harmless links, and AgentDojo, a public benchmark we did not write. A program, not a person, scores each run by checking the final mailbox.

Key line: Frozen first, then tested on attacks the defenses never saw.

## 9. Development: attacks 45% → 0%, no normal task lost

First, development. With no defense, 45.4% of attacks worked. With any of the four defenses, none did. (pause) The zeros are earned: under D1h+D2 the model still tried the attacker's action 8 times, and every attempt was blocked. And D1h+D2 completed 89.3% of normal tasks, the same as no defense.

Key line: Every defense reached zero, and D1h+D2 lost no normal task.

## 10. Held-out: attacks 22% → 0%, three runs

Now the real test: attacks written after the freeze. Pooled over three runs, 21.8% of held-out attacks worked with no defense, and 0.0% under every defense; under D1h+D2 the model still tried the attacker's action 19 times, all blocked. (pause) One honest caveat: the 18 attacks we wrote ourselves never worked, not even with no defense: 0/54. So they don't test the defenses; all 38 successes came from the 40 new LLMail-Inject emails, 31.7% of them with no defense. (pause) Normal tasks: D1h+D2 91.7% against 89.3% with no defense, +2.4 points. Paired test against no defense: p = 7.3 × 10⁻¹².

Key line: Zero held-out attacks got through, and the attacks that worked were real LLMail emails.

## 11. Does it carry over? A second model and AgentDojo

Does this carry over? (pause) First, a second model family: Qwen2.5-7B on the same held-out set, one run. With no defense 29.3% of attacks worked; with a defense, at most 0.0%. (pause) Second, AgentDojo's workspace suite, a different benchmark with its own tools and attack. Its stock attack almost never worked on our model: 2 of 160 pairs with no defense, so this run cannot show protection. What it does show is cost: the defenses ran unchanged on tasks we did not write, and D1h+D2 completed 30.0% of tasks against 27.5% without a defense; Dual-LLM managed 12.5%. One caveat: D2's policy there comes from each task's ground truth, an upper bound. We also tried the 3 other AgentDojo attacks with no defense on 24 tasks each: no successes, although the injection reached the model in most episodes. So the model ignores these attacks; it is not our plumbing.

Key line: Safe on a second model; on AgentDojo, no utility cost, but its attack was too weak here to test safety.

## 12. CAMEL-AI in our sandbox: new agent, same gate

The professor asked us to bring CAMEL-AI into the sandbox. CAMEL-AI is a popular open-source framework for building AI agents. (pause) We swapped our own agent loop for CAMEL-AI's ChatAgent, and kept everything else the same: same model, same gateway, same container, and every tool call still goes through our gate. The screenshot is the scripted agent that always obeys the attack: with no defense the forward goes through; with any of our defenses it is blocked; and Alex's task is still done. (pause) The full held-out run with CAMEL-AI is running now; the results will be in the report. Careful with the name: CAMEL-AI, the agent framework, is not CaMeL, a defense from Google DeepMind. CaMeL is future work.

Key line: The gate does not care which agent is behind it.

## 13. The cost we almost missed: harmless links

Our first benchmark had no normal task with a link in it, so it could not show this cost. (pause) D1h blocks any link copied from an email into a new message, because it cannot tell a colleague's Zoom link from a phishing link. Asking for the link and forwarding the email still always work. (pause) We tried an exploratory fix, D1h-L, after the freeze: a link may go out if the user asks for a link, names the email, and that email came from a contact. It recovers the flow and let no attack through, but a compromised contact account would defeat it. (pause) The reply row fails for a different reason: the model's first move was a reply to an email id that does not exist. Without a defense it got 'no such email' and recovered; with a defense it got a plain refusal and gave up. How a defense refuses matters. Across all 120 link episodes per config.

Key line: Measure the cost on harmless work, not only on attacks.

## 14. Hypotheses scorecard

Scorecard on the held-out set. (pause) The undefended attack rate is 21.8%, below our 30% validity bar; on the LLMail part alone it is 31.7%, because our own attacks never worked. H1, safety: met. H2, usefulness: met, a change of +2.4 points. (pause) Against Dual-LLM: both stopped the same number of attacks, so we cannot call ours safer; the difference is usefulness: D1h+D2 completes significantly more normal tasks.

Key line: H1 met, H2 met, on attacks we never saw.

## 15. What this does not show yet, and what is next

Rui again. What our results do not show yet. (pause) First, every attack we ran is fixed. None adapts to our rules, and an attacker who knows them has targets. Second, the link cost Khadijah showed. (pause) Two pieces of related work we found while following up the consultation. CaMeL, from Google DeepMind, is a defense: the model turns the user's request into a small program and the system tracks where every piece of data came from. It is close to our provenance idea, but stricter, and comparing against it is the natural next step. SETA, from the CAMEL-AI team, is a set of environments for agents that work in a terminal; it has no prompt-injection tests yet, so putting our gate around shell tools would be new work.

Key line: Strong on fixed attacks; adaptive attackers are the open question.

## 16. Takeaways

Three takeaways. (pause) One: decide outside the model. Checking each action in code stopped every attack we ran, with no extra model calls. Two: the two checks do different jobs. D2 removes what the task doesn't need; D1h catches attacker content riding inside an action the user asked for. Three: measure harmless work too. Our first benchmark could not see that D1h blocks copied links. Thank you.

Key line: Trace the data, gate the action, and measure what it costs.
